docs.text:
Welcome to the VLSI & Embedded Systems Engineering Documentation Hub. This repository serves as a centralized, rigorous technical reference, lab repository, and self-testing platform covering foundational computing infrastructure, hardware description languages, ASIC physical design, and verification methodologies.

Curriculum Scope & Context

The depth, sequencing, and practical problem sets curated across these modules reflect the PGCP-VLSI curriculum standard. Concepts are presented with clear theoretical depth, architectural diagrams, syntax cheat sheets, and real-world scripting patterns.

docs.title: 🎯 Why This Documentation Exists
docs.text:
Modern VLSI front-end and back-end design flows rely heavily on command-line automation, Unix pipelines, configuration scripts, and scalable simulation setups. This knowledge base was built to:

  1. Establish Strong Foundations: Provide deep conceptual breakdowns of the Linux kernel, POSIX filesystem standards, system calls, and network diagnostics required for EDA tool server environments.
  2. Master Scripting Automation: Bridge the gap between interactive terminal commands and production-grade Bash scripting, regular expressions, sed, and awk text processing for EDA log parsing.
  3. Continuous Self-Evaluation: Pair every theoretical concept with structured assignment question banks, interactive collapsible solutions, and extensive multiple-choice assessments.

docs.title: Assignment 01: Linux Basics, Directory Operations & Permissions
docs.text:
Comprehensive self-testing question bank covering User/Group identification (id, whoami), directory tree navigation (pwd, cd, mkdir -p), file inspection, octal/symbolic permissions (chmod), ownership (chown, chgrp), and manual pages (man).

Interactive Self-Study Mode

Attempt each question in your terminal or mentally before expanding the solution block to review the detailed four-option technical breakdown.

docs.title: Question 1: Which command is used to display both the numeric User ID (UID), primary Group ID (GID), and all supplementary groups of the currently logged-in user?
docs.text:
• (A) whoami
  • (B) id
  • (C) groups
  • (D) uname -u
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) id

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Displays only the effective username string (e.g., 'saichand'), without numeric UID, GID, or group lists. - (B) Correct. 'id' outputs the complete identity string including numeric UID, GID, and all associated supplementary groups. - (C) Displays only group names associated with the user, omitting the numeric UID, GID, and username. - (D) 'uname' reports kernel and OS architecture information; the '-u' flag is invalid.

docs.title: Question 2: Which command and option creates a 3-level nested directory structure 'mydir/Subdir1/Subdir2' in a single command without failing if parent directories do not exist?
docs.text:
• (A) mkdir -r mydir/Subdir1/Subdir2
  • (B) mkdir -p mydir/Subdir1/Subdir2
  • (C) mkdir -f mydir/Subdir1/Subdir2
  • (D) md -all mydir/Subdir1/Subdir2
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) mkdir -p mydir/Subdir1/Subdir2

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) '-r' is used for recursive operations in commands like 'rm' and 'cp', but is not a valid parent-creation option in 'mkdir'. - (B) Correct. The '-p' (parents) flag creates intermediate parent directories as needed and does not return an error if directories already exist. - (C) '-f' (force) is not a valid flag for 'mkdir'. - (D) 'md' is a DOS/Windows command; Linux uses 'mkdir'.

docs.title: Question 3: To modify the permissions of a file 'ctest' such that the User has Read, Write, and Execute (rwx), the Group has Read and Execute (r-x), and Others have No permissions (---), which command is correct?
docs.text:
• (A) chmod 750 ctest
  • (B) chmod 755 ctest
  • (C) chmod 640 ctest
  • (D) chmod 700 ctest
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) chmod 750 ctest

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. In octal: User rwx (4+2+1=7), Group r-x (4+0+1=5), Others --- (0+0+0=0) gives 750. - (B) 755 gives Others read and execute (r-x) permissions instead of no permissions (---). - (C) 640 sets User to rw- (no execute) and Group to r-- (no execute). - (D) 700 sets Group to --- (no permissions), whereas Group requires r-x.

docs.title: Question 4: Which command changes both the owner user to 'saichand' and the owning group to 'vlsidevs' for the file 'top.v' in a single command?
docs.text:
• (A) chgrp saichand:vlsidevs top.v
  • (B) chown saichand.vlsidevs top.v
  • (C) chown saichand:vlsidevs top.v
  • (D) chmod saichand:vlsidevs top.v
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (C) chown saichand:vlsidevs top.v

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) 'chgrp' modifies group ownership only and does not accept user:group syntax. - (B) While dot syntax was historically supported, colon syntax 'user:group' is the POSIX standard across modern Linux. - (C) Correct. 'chown user:group filename' updates both the user owner and group owner atomically. - (D) 'chmod' alters permission mode bits (read/write/execute), not file ownership.

docs.title: Question 5: What is the difference between running 'cd ~' and 'cd -' in a Bash terminal?
docs.text:
• (A) 'cd ~' goes to root directory '/', while 'cd -' goes to home directory.
  • (B) 'cd ~' goes to user home directory ($HOME), while 'cd -' switches to the previous working directory ($OLDPWD).
  • (C) 'cd ~' creates a temporary directory, while 'cd -' deletes the current directory.
  • (D) 'cd ~' and 'cd -' are identical aliases for navigating up one directory level.
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) 'cd ~' goes to user home directory ($HOME), while 'cd -' switches to the previous working directory ($OLDPWD).

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Root directory is reached via 'cd /', not 'cd ~'. - (B) Correct. The tilde '~' expands to $HOME, while the hyphen '-' expands to the previous working directory stored in $OLDPWD. - (C) Neither command creates or deletes directories. - (D) Navigating up one level is performed using 'cd ..'.

docs.title: Question 6: Which command lists all files including hidden files, sorted with the most recently modified files at the bottom of the terminal output?
docs.text:
• (A) ls -la
  • (B) ls -latr
  • (C) ls -lR
  • (D) ls -lhS
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) ls -latr

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) 'ls -la' lists all files including hidden files, but sorts them alphabetically. - (B) Correct. '-l' (long format), '-a' (all/hidden), '-t' (sort by modification time), and '-r' (reverse order) puts newest files at the bottom. - (C) 'ls -lR' lists directories recursively. - (D) 'ls -lhS' sorts files by file size in descending order.

docs.title: Question 7: How do you view section 1 of the man page for the 'passwd' user command rather than section 5 for the '/etc/passwd' file format?
docs.text:
• (A) man passwd
  • (B) man 1 passwd
  • (C) man 5 passwd
  • (D) man -a passwd
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) man 1 passwd

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Running 'man passwd' without a section number defaults to the first matching section, which may be ambiguous. - (B) Correct. 'man 1 passwd' explicitly requests Section 1 (User executable commands). - (C) 'man 5 passwd' opens Section 5 (File formats and conventions, specifically /etc/passwd). - (D) 'man -a passwd' displays all matching man sections in sequential order.

docs.title: Question 8: Which command creates an empty file named 'simulation.log' if it does not exist, or updates its access/modification timestamps if it already exists?
docs.text:
• (A) make simulation.log
  • (B) create simulation.log
  • (C) touch simulation.log
  • (D) new simulation.log
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (C) touch simulation.log

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) 'make' is a build automation tool that reads Makefiles, not a file creation utility. - (B) 'create' is not a standard Linux command. - (C) Correct. 'touch' creates a 0-byte file if non-existent or updates inode timestamps if existing. - (D) 'new' is not a valid Linux file utility.

docs.title: Question 9: When moving a directory 'mydir' into a new directory 'mydir1' using 'mv mydir mydir1', what happens if 'mydir1' already exists as a directory?
docs.text:
• (A) The command fails with a directory overwrite error.
  • (B) 'mydir' is moved inside 'mydir1' as a subdirectory ('mydir1/mydir').
  • (C) 'mydir1' is deleted and replaced with 'mydir'.
  • (D) The contents of 'mydir' are merged with 'mydir1' and 'mydir' is deleted.
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) 'mydir' is moved inside 'mydir1' as a subdirectory ('mydir1/mydir').

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) 'mv' does not error when moving into an existing target directory. - (B) Correct. If the destination is an existing directory, 'mv' places the source directory inside it. - (C) 'mv' will not overwrite an existing non-empty directory with another directory. - (D) Directory merging is performed using 'rsync' or 'cp -r', not standard 'mv'.

docs.title: Question 10: Which symbolic command grants execute permission to the User, removes write permission from Group, and assigns read-only permission to Others for file 'script.sh'?
docs.text:
• (A) chmod u+x,g-w,o=r script.sh
  • (B) chmod u+x;g-w;o=r script.sh
  • (C) chmod u=x,g=w,o=r script.sh
  • (D) chmod +x -w =r script.sh
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) chmod u+x,g-w,o=r script.sh

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. Comma-separated symbolic clauses 'u+x,g-w,o=r' apply the exact requested modifications. - (B) Semicolons separate distinct shell commands rather than clauses within 'chmod'. - (C) 'u=x' sets execute ONLY for user (revoking existing read/write), rather than adding execute (+x). - (D) Missing category qualifiers (u/g/o) causes ambiguous application across umask.

docs.title: Question 11: Which command removes a non-empty directory 'old_build' and all of its contents without prompting for confirmation?
docs.text:
• (A) rmdir old_build
  • (B) rm -r -f old_build
  • (C) del /s old_build
  • (D) erase -rf old_build
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) rm -r -f old_build

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) 'rmdir' strictly removes empty directories; it fails with 'Directory not empty' on populated folders. - (B) Correct. 'rm -rf' recursively (-r) and forcefully (-f) removes files and subdirectories without interactive prompts. - (C) 'del /s' is Windows cmd syntax. - (D) 'erase' is not a standard Linux command.

docs.title: Question 12: What is the result of executing 'chmod 644 design.v' on an RTL source file?
docs.text:
• (A) Owner: Read/Write, Group: Read-Only, Others: Read-Only
  • (B) Owner: Read/Write/Execute, Group: Read-Only, Others: None
  • (C) Owner: Read-Only, Group: Read-Only, Others: Read/Write
  • (D) Owner: Read/Write, Group: Read/Write, Others: Read/Write
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) Owner: Read/Write, Group: Read-Only, Others: Read-Only

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 6 = 4+2 (rw-), 4 = 4+0 (r--), 4 = 4+0 (r--). - (B) Read/Write/Execute is octal 7, not 6. - (C) Read-Only across owner is octal 446, not 644. - (D) Read/Write across all categories is octal 666.

docs.title: Question 13: Which command displays the manual page summary description for a keyword, equivalent to 'man -k'?
docs.text:
• (A) whatis
  • (B) apropos
  • (C) whereis
  • (D) which
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) apropos

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) 'whatis' searches for complete exact command names in the whatis database, equivalent to 'man -f'. - (B) Correct. 'apropos keyword' searches description strings across all man pages, identical to 'man -k keyword'. - (C) 'whereis' locates binary, source, and man page file paths on disk. - (D) 'which' locates executable binaries in the user's $PATH.

docs.title: Question 14: If a user attempts to execute a shell script 'test.sh' with permissions '-rw-r--r--', what error is returned by the shell?
docs.text:
• (A) Segmentation fault
  • (B) Permission denied
  • (C) Command not found
  • (D) Bad interpreter error
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) Permission denied

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Segmentation fault indicates invalid memory access by a compiled binary. - (B) Correct. The file lacks the execute bit ('x') for the executing user, triggering a 'Permission denied' error. - (C) 'Command not found' occurs when an executable is not in $PATH or the specified relative path is wrong. - (D) 'Bad interpreter error' occurs when the shebang line points to a non-existent binary.

docs.title: Question 15: Which command creates a hard link named 'link_top.v' pointing to 'top.v'?
docs.text:
• (A) ln -s top.v link_top.v
  • (B) ln top.v link_top.v
  • (C) link -h top.v link_top.v
  • (D) cp -l top.v link_top.v
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) ln top.v link_top.v

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) '-s' creates a symbolic (soft) link, not a hard link. - (B) Correct. 'ln source target' creates a hard link by default sharing the exact same inode number. - (C) 'link' takes exactly two arguments without flags. - (D) While 'cp -l' can link instead of copying, standard 'ln' is the POSIX utility.

docs.title: Assignment 02: File Operations, Text Filtering & Search Pipelines
docs.text:
Practical questions covering pipelines (|), redirection (>, >>, tee), grep regular expressions, stream editing with sed, column extraction with cut, and find actions.

Interactive Self-Study Mode

Attempt each question in your terminal or mentally before expanding the solution block to review the detailed four-option technical breakdown.

docs.title: Question 1: Which pipeline counts the number of unique user login shells listed in '/etc/passwd'?
docs.text:
• (A) cut -d ':' -f 7 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq | wc -l
  • (B) cut -d ':' -f 1 /etc/passwd | uniq -c
  • (C) grep 'bin' /etc/passwd | wc -w
  • (D) sort /etc/passwd | cut -f 7 | count
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) cut -d ':' -f 7 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq | wc -l

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'cut -d : -f 7' extracts the shell field, 'sort' groups identical shells, 'uniq' deduplicates them, and 'wc -l' counts total unique entries. - (B) Field 1 extracts usernames, not shells; and uniq without sort fails to deduplicate non-adjacent duplicates. - (C) Filters for lines containing 'bin' and counts total words, not unique shells. - (D) 'cut -f 7' defaults to tab delimiter (failing on colon-separated /etc/passwd), and 'count' is not a standard Unix command.

docs.title: Question 2: Which command searches for the pattern 'CRITICAL_TIMING' in all '.rpt' files under the current directory tree, ignoring case and showing line numbers?
docs.text:
• (A) find . -name '*.rpt' | grep -i 'CRITICAL_TIMING'
  • (B) grep -rni --include='*.rpt' 'CRITICAL_TIMING' .
  • (C) locate -i 'CRITICAL_TIMING' *.rpt
  • (D) sed -n '/CRITICAL_TIMING/p' *.rpt
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) grep -rni --include='*.rpt' 'CRITICAL_TIMING' .

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Grep would match against the filename paths emitted by find, rather than searching inside the contents of the report files. - (B) Correct. '-r' (recursive), '-n' (line numbers), '-i' (case-insensitive), and '--include=.rpt' searches inside all matching reports efficiently. - (C) 'locate' searches filenames in a database index, not file contents. - (D)* 'sed' does not perform recursive directory traversal and would not print line numbers by default.

docs.title: Question 3: What is the key functional difference between output redirection operators '>' and '>>'?
docs.text:
• (A) '>' appends to an existing file, while '>>' truncates/overwrites the file.
  • (B) '>' redirects standard output, while '>>' redirects standard error.
  • (C) '>' overwrites the target file, while '>>' appends data to the end of the file.
  • (D) '>' creates a temporary file, while '>>' creates a permanent file.
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (C) '>' overwrites the target file, while '>>' appends data to the end of the file.

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) This reverses the true meanings: '>' overwrites, '>>' appends. - (B) Both operate on standard output (FD 1) by default; stderr is redirected via '2>' or '2>>'. - (C) Correct. Single chevron '>' truncates/creates the file, whereas double chevron '>>' appends new lines to existing content. - (D) Both operators operate directly on standard filesystem targets.

docs.title: Question 4: Which command finds all regular files in '/home/student' larger than 50 Megabytes modified within the last 7 days?
docs.text:
• (A) find /home/student -type f -size +50M -mtime -7
  • (B) find /home/student -type d -size 50M -mtime +7
  • (C) search /home/student -files -size >50MB -days <7
  • (D) find /home/student -name '*.v' -size 50M -ctime 7
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) find /home/student -type f -size +50M -mtime -7

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. '-type f' matches regular files, '-size +50M' matches greater than 50MB, and '-mtime -7' matches modified less than 7 days ago. - (B) '-type d' searches for directories, and '-mtime +7' searches for files older than 7 days. - (C) 'search' is not a standard Linux command. - (D) Constrains search to '*.v' and exact 50M/7 days rather than greater/less than thresholds.

docs.title: Question 5: Which 'sed' command substitutes all occurrences of 'wire [31:0]' with 'logic [31:0]' globally in 'design.v' and writes changes directly to the file?
docs.text:
• (A) sed 's/wire [31:0]/logic [31:0]/' design.v
  • (B) sed -i 's/wire [31:0]/logic [31:0]/g' design.v
  • (C) sed -e 'replace wire logic' design.v
  • (D) grep -v 'wire' design.v > design.v
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) sed -i 's/wire [31:0]/logic [31:0]/g' design.v

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Missing '-i' (prints to stdout without saving to disk) and missing 'g' flag (replaces only the first occurrence per line). - (B) Correct. '-i' enables in-place file modification, and 'g' flag replaces all occurrences on each line. - (C) 'replace' is not valid sed command syntax. - (D) Redirecting to the same input file 'design.v' truncates the file to 0 bytes before grep reads it.

docs.title: Question 6: Which command creates a compressed archive named 'vlsi_backup.tar.gz' containing the 'rtl/' directory?
docs.text:
• (A) tar -cvf vlsi_backup.tar.gz rtl/
  • (B) tar -czvf vlsi_backup.tar.gz rtl/
  • (C) gzip -tar vlsi_backup.tar.gz rtl/
  • (D) zip -tar vlsi_backup.tar.gz rtl/
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) tar -czvf vlsi_backup.tar.gz rtl/

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) '-cvf' creates an uncompressed tar archive despite the '.tar.gz' extension name. - (B) Correct. '-c' (create), '-z' (gzip compression), '-v' (verbose), and '-f' (archive filename) creates a compressed gzip tarball. - (C) 'gzip' does not accept a directory or '-tar' flag directly. - (D) 'zip' creates '.zip' format files, not tar.gz archives.

docs.title: Question 7: How do you extract lines 20 through 35 from a 1000-line simulation log file 'run.log'?
docs.text:
• (A) head -n 35 run.log | tail -n 16
  • (B) head -n 20 run.log | tail -n 35
  • (C) tail -n +20 run.log | head -n 35
  • (D) cat run.log | cut -l 20-35
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) head -n 35 run.log | tail -n 16

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'head -n 35' takes the first 35 lines, and piping to 'tail -n 16' extracts the last 16 lines (lines 20 to 35 inclusive). - (B) This takes the first 20 lines and then the last 35 of those, producing only lines 1 to 20. - (C) 'head -n 35' on 'tail -n +20' extracts 35 lines (lines 20 through 54), not 16 lines. - (D) 'cut -l' is invalid flag syntax for cut.

docs.title: Question 8: Which tool and argument deletes all carriage-return characters ('\r') from a DOS-formatted text file?
docs.text:
• (A) tr -d '\r' < dos_file.txt > unix_file.txt
  • (B) cut -d '\r' dos_file.txt
  • (C) sed 'delete \r' dos_file.txt
  • (D) wc -d '\r' dos_file.txt
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) tr -d '\r' < dos_file.txt > unix_file.txt

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'tr -d \r' deletes all carriage return characters from the standard input stream. - (B) 'cut -d' specifies field delimiter for column extraction, not character deletion. - (C) Sed delete command requires '/\r/d' address notation. - (D) 'wc' is a word/line counting utility and does not support deletion.

docs.title: Question 9: Which command displays only lines in 'file1.txt' and 'file2.txt' that are unique to 'file1.txt' (suppressing common lines and lines unique to file2), assuming both files are sorted?
docs.text:
• (A) diff -u file1.txt file2.txt
  • (B) comm -23 file1.txt file2.txt
  • (C) cmp file1.txt file2.txt
  • (D) uniq -u file1.txt file2.txt
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) comm -23 file1.txt file2.txt

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) 'diff -u' outputs unified difference format showing added and removed lines together. - (B) Correct. 'comm' outputs 3 columns: (1) unique to file1, (2) unique to file2, (3) common. '-23' suppresses columns 2 and 3, outputting column 1 only. - (C) 'cmp' performs byte-by-byte comparison and stops at the first differing byte. - (D) 'uniq -u' operates on a single file stream, not two distinct files.

docs.title: Question 10: What is the function of the 'tee' utility in a Linux pipeline?
docs.text:
• (A) It terminates execution if an error occurs in the pipeline.
  • (B) It duplicates standard input to standard output and simultaneously writes it to one or more files.
  • (C) It tests the network bandwidth between two remote servers.
  • (D) It converts text files from ASCII to UTF-8 encoding.
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) It duplicates standard input to standard output and simultaneously writes it to one or more files.

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Error termination in bash is configured via 'set -e', not 'tee'. - (B) Correct. 'tee' acts as a T-splitter, sending stream output to both stdout (terminal) and specified log files. - (C) Network bandwidth testing is performed with 'iperf', not 'tee'. - (D) Character encoding conversion is handled by 'iconv'.

docs.title: Assignment 03: User Administration, ACLs, Process Control & Crontab
docs.text:
Questions covering user/group management (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow), POSIX ACLs (setfacl), process states, signals (kill -9), and crontab task automation.

Interactive Self-Study Mode

Attempt each question in your terminal or mentally before expanding the solution block to review the detailed four-option technical breakdown.

docs.title: Question 1: Which command creates a new group named 'vlsidevs' and then adds existing user 'student1' to it without removing them from their other supplementary groups?
docs.text:
• (A) groupadd vlsidevs && usermod -g vlsidevs student1
  • (B) groupadd vlsidevs && usermod -aG vlsidevs student1
  • (C) groupcreate vlsidevs && useradd -G vlsidevs student1
  • (D) addgroup vlsidevs && passwd -g vlsidevs student1
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) groupadd vlsidevs && usermod -aG vlsidevs student1

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) '-g' replaces the user's PRIMARY group rather than appending to supplementary groups. - (B) Correct. 'groupadd' creates the group, and 'usermod -aG' appends (-a) the user to the supplementary group (-G). - (C) 'groupcreate' is not a valid Linux command, and 'useradd' is used to create new users, not modify existing ones. - (D) 'passwd -g' is invalid syntax for group membership.

docs.title: Question 2: Where are encrypted user passwords and password expiration metadata securely stored in a standard Linux system?
docs.text:
• (A) /etc/passwd
  • (B) /etc/shadow
  • (C) /etc/security
  • (D) /var/log/auth.log
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) /etc/shadow

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) '/etc/passwd' is world-readable and stores account metadata with an 'x' placeholder for passwords. - (B) Correct. '/etc/shadow' is readable strictly by root (mode 640 or 600) and contains salted password hashes and aging policies. - (C) '/etc/security' contains PAM configuration files, not user password hashes. - (D) '/var/log/auth.log' contains authentication audit logs.

docs.title: Question 3: Which command grants user 'alice' read and write access on 'shared_netlist.v' using POSIX Access Control Lists (ACLs)?
docs.text:
• (A) chmod u:alice:rw shared_netlist.v
  • (B) setfacl -m u:alice:rw shared_netlist.v
  • (C) getfacl -set alice=rw shared_netlist.v
  • (D) chown alice:rw shared_netlist.v
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) setfacl -m u:alice:rw shared_netlist.v

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) 'chmod' only accepts standard UGO categories (u/g/o), not named individual usernames. - (B) Correct. 'setfacl -m u:username:perms file' modifies the ACL to grant specific permissions to named users. - (C) 'getfacl' is used to view ACLs, not set or modify them. - (D) 'chown' modifies file ownership, not permission masks.

docs.title: Question 4: What is the signal number and characteristic of SIGKILL?
docs.text:
• (A) Signal 15; allows the process to catch the signal and perform clean termination.
  • (B) Signal 2; sent when the user presses Ctrl+C in the terminal.
  • (C) Signal 9; cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored, resulting in immediate kernel-level termination.
  • (D) Signal 1; reloads daemon configuration files without stopping the process.
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (C) Signal 9; cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored, resulting in immediate kernel-level termination.

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Signal 15 is SIGTERM (graceful termination). - (B) Signal 2 is SIGINT (interrupt from keyboard). - (C) Correct. SIGKILL is Signal 9 and is handled directly by the kernel scheduler; processes cannot intercept or ignore it. - (D) Signal 1 is SIGHUP (hangup/reload).

docs.title: Question 5: Which crontab entry runs a script '/opt/scripts/backup.sh' every Monday through Friday at exactly 6:30 PM (18:30)?
docs.text:
• (A) 30 18 * * 1-5 /opt/scripts/backup.sh
  • (B) 18 30 * * 1-5 /opt/scripts/backup.sh
  • (C) * 18 30 * 1,5 /opt/scripts/backup.sh
  • (D) 30 6 * * Mon-Fri /opt/scripts/backup.sh
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) 30 18 * * 1-5 /opt/scripts/backup.sh

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. Fields: Minute=30, Hour=18, DayOfMonth=, Month=, DayOfWeek=1-5 (Monday-Friday). - (B) Reverses minute and hour (would run at 18 minutes past 6:00 PM). - (C) Runs every minute during hour 18 on day 30 of the month. - (D) Hour 6 is 6:00 AM (06:00), not 6:30 PM (18:30).

docs.text:
Questions covering IPv4 CIDR subnetting, socket inspection (ss), reachability diagnostics (ping, traceroute), SSH key authentication, scp, and .bashrc environment profiles.

docs.title: Question 1: How many usable host IP addresses are available in a subnet configured with CIDR prefix /28 (subnet mask 255.255.255.240)?
docs.text:
• (A) 16
  • (B) 14
  • (C) 30
  • (D) 6
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (B) 14

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) 16 is the total number of IP addresses (2^(32-28) = 16), including Network ID and Broadcast ID. - (B) Correct. Usable hosts = 2^(32-28) - 2 = 16 - 2 = 14. - (C) 30 hosts corresponds to a /27 subnet mask (255.255.255.224). - (D) 6 hosts corresponds to a /29 subnet mask (255.255.255.248).

docs.title: Question 2: Which modern command displays all listening TCP and UDP sockets along with their process names and PIDs?
docs.text:
• (A) ss -tulnp
  • (B) ip route show
  • (C) ping -tulnp
  • (D) ifconfig -listening
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) ss -tulnp

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'ss' (socket statistics) with '-t' (TCP), '-u' (UDP), '-l' (listening), '-n' (numeric ports), and '-p' (process ID) inspects listening sockets. - (B) 'ip route' displays routing tables, not socket connections. - (C) 'ping' sends ICMP echo requests and does not take socket flags. - (D) 'ifconfig' does not have a '-listening' option.

docs.title: Question 3: Which startup configuration file is executed for interactive, non-login Bash shell sessions for a specific user?
docs.text:
• (A) ~/.bashrc
  • (B) /etc/profile
  • (C) ~/.bash_profile
  • (D) /etc/environment
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) ~/.bashrc

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. '~/.bashrc' is executed whenever a new interactive subshell or terminal tab is opened. - (B) '/etc/profile' is the system-wide login shell initialization script. - (C) '~/.bash_profile' is executed only during initial user login (e.g. SSH login or console login). - (D) '/etc/environment' defines system-wide environment key-value pairs, not shell scripts.

docs.title: Question 4: Which command copies a directory 'rtl_src/' recursively from a local machine to a remote server at IP 192.168.1.50 under '/home/user/' via SSH?
docs.text:
• (A) scp -r rtl_src/ user@192.168.1.50:/home/user/
  • (B) cp -remote rtl_src/ user@192.168.1.50:/home/user/
  • (C) ssh cp -r rtl_src/ user@192.168.1.50:/home/user/
  • (D) ftp -r rtl_src/ user@192.168.1.50:/home/user/
Answer & Detailed Technical Explanation (Click to Expand)

Correct Answer: (A) scp -r rtl_src/ user@192.168.1.50:/home/user/

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'scp -r' uses the SSH protocol to recursively copy files securely between hosts. - (B) 'cp' only operates on locally mounted filesystems. - (C) 'ssh' executes commands remotely on the destination server rather than transferring local source files. - (D) 'ftp' is an unencrypted legacy protocol that requires interactive commands or separate batch scripting.

docs.title: Assignment 05: Shell Scripting Automation Lab Problem Sets
docs.text:
A comprehensive 20-problem laboratory assessment divided into Part 1: Simple Automation Scripts (user/group creation, file permissions, directory trees, timestamped backups) and Part 2: Conditional Statements & Validation (user validation, file test operators, arithmetic comparisons, disk usage monitors).

Interactive Self-Study & Script Testing

Write each shell script in your Ubuntu terminal and test with real arguments before expanding the solution box to review the code breakdown and alternative approaches.

docs.title: 📑 Part 1: Simple Shell Scripting Automation
Question 1: Lab 1.1: Write a shell script to create a new user account named 'emp1' with a home directory and set an initial password.
docs.text:
• (A) sudo useradd -m emp1 && echo 'emp1:Password123' | sudo chpasswd
  • (B) sudo adduser --no-home emp1
  • (C) sudo usercreate emp1 -p Password123
  • (D) echo 'emp1' >> /etc/passwd
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) sudo useradd -m emp1 && echo 'emp1:Password123' | sudo chpasswd

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'useradd -m emp1' creates the user with a home directory in /home/emp1, and 'chpasswd' batch-sets the initial password securely in non-interactive scripts. - (B) '--no-home' explicitly prevents home directory creation. - (C) 'usercreate' is not a standard Linux command. - (D) Directly appending to /etc/passwd bypasses password encryption, shadow hashing, GID generation, and home directory initialization.

docs.title: Question 2: Lab 1.2: Write a shell script that creates a new group called 'hr' and adds an existing user (passed as $1) to that group.
docs.text:
• (A) sudo groupadd hr && sudo usermod -aG hr "$1"
  • (B) sudo groupadd hr && sudo useradd -g hr "$1"
  • (C) sudo addgroup hr "$1"
  • (D) sudo usermod -g hr "$1"
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) sudo groupadd hr && sudo usermod -aG hr "$1"

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'groupadd hr' creates the group, and 'usermod -aG hr "$1"' safely appends the user to the secondary group without overwriting existing memberships. - (B) 'useradd' is used to create new users, not modify existing user accounts. - (C) 'addgroup hr "$1"' syntax varies across distributions and may fail without group pre-existence. - (D) '-g' replaces the primary group rather than adding 'hr' as a supplementary group.

docs.title: Question 3: Lab 1.3: Write a shell script that displays the UID, GID, and all group memberships of a user whose username is supplied as $1.
docs.text:
• (A) id "$1"
  • (B) whoami "$1"
  • (C) groups --all "$1"
  • (D) cat /etc/passwd | grep "$1" | cut -d: -f3
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) id "$1"

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'id username' outputs numeric UID, GID, and all associated group names and GIDs in standard format. - (B) 'whoami' takes no arguments and prints only the current effective username. - (C) 'groups' displays group names only, omitting numeric UID and primary GID. - (D) Extracts only the UID field, omitting GID and secondary group memberships.

docs.title: Question 4: Lab 1.4: Write a shell script that creates 'data.txt' and sets its permissions to 'rwxr--r--' (Owner: rwx, Group: r--, Others: r--).
docs.text:
• (A) touch data.txt && chmod 744 data.txt
  • (B) touch data.txt && chmod 755 data.txt
  • (C) touch data.txt && chmod 644 data.txt
  • (D) make data.txt && chmod u=rwx,go=r data.txt
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) touch data.txt && chmod 744 data.txt

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'touch data.txt' creates the file and octal 744 sets User=rwx (7), Group=r-- (4), Others=r-- (4). - (B) 755 grants execute permission to Group and Others (r-x). - (C) 644 sets User to rw- (missing execute bit). - (D) 'make' is a build utility, not a file creation tool.

docs.title: Question 5: Lab 1.5: Write a shell script that changes the owner and group of 'report.txt' to a given username ($1) and group name ($2).
docs.text:
• (A) sudo chown "$1:$2" report.txt
  • (B) sudo chgrp "$1:$2" report.txt
  • (C) sudo chmod "$1:$2" report.txt
  • (D) sudo chown "$1" report.txt && sudo chown "$2" report.txt
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) sudo chown "$1:$2" report.txt

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'chown user:group filename' updates both the user owner and group owner in a single atomic command. - (B) 'chgrp' modifies group ownership only and does not accept user:group syntax. - (C) 'chmod' changes permission bits (rwx), not ownership. - (D) The second command would attempt to set the user owner to '$2' rather than changing the group.

docs.title: Question 6: Lab 1.6: Write a shell script that displays a given file's permissions in both symbolic form (e.g., -rw-r--r--) and numeric/octal form (e.g., 644).
docs.text:
• (A) ls -l "$1" | awk '{print $1}'; stat -c "%a" "$1"
  • (B) stat -c "%A %a" "$1"
  • (C) ls -l "$1" && chmod -v "$1"
  • (D) Both A and B are valid solutions.
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (D) Both A and B are valid solutions.

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Valid. 'ls -l' extracts symbolic mode via awk, and 'stat -c %a' prints octal mode. - (B) Valid. 'stat -c "%A %a"' directly outputs symbolic (%A) and octal (%a) permissions in a single command. - (C) 'chmod -v' modifies permissions rather than simply displaying existing values. - (D) Correct. Both A and B are accurate implementations.

docs.title: Question 7: Lab 1.7: Write a shell script that creates the directory structure '/dbda/project/{src,bin,docs}' in a single command and lists the structure.
docs.text:
• (A) mkdir -p /dbda/project/{src,bin,docs} && ls -l /dbda/project
  • (B) mkdir /dbda/project/src /dbda/project/bin /dbda/project/docs
  • (C) mkdir -r /dbda/project/{src,bin,docs}
  • (D) create -p /dbda/project/{src,bin,docs}
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) mkdir -p /dbda/project/{src,bin,docs} && ls -l /dbda/project

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'mkdir -p' with bash brace expansion creates intermediate parent directories and all three subdirectories, followed by 'ls -l'. - (B) Fails if parent directories '/dbda' and '/dbda/project' do not already exist. - (C) '-r' is invalid for mkdir; the parent creation flag is '-p'. - (D) 'create' is not a standard Linux command.

docs.title: Question 8: Lab 1.8: Write a shell script that accepts a username as $1 and displays that user's home directory path and login shell.
docs.text:
• (A) getent passwd "$1" | cut -d: -f6,7
  • (B) grep "^$1:" /etc/passwd | awk -F: '{print "Home:", $6, "Shell:", $7}'
  • (C) finger "$1"
  • (D) Both A and B are standard, robust solutions.
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (D) Both A and B are standard, robust solutions.

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Valid. 'getent passwd' queries the NSS database (supporting local and LDAP users) and fields 6 & 7 are home and shell. - (B) Valid. Anchored grep '^$1:' on /etc/passwd extracts fields 6 (home directory) and 7 (login shell) via awk. - (C) 'finger' is a legacy utility not installed by default on modern Linux distributions. - (D) Correct. Both A and B provide robust, production-grade implementations.

docs.title: Question 9: Lab 1.9: Write a shell script that takes an old filename ($1) and new filename ($2), renames the file, and displays its permissions.
docs.text:
• (A) mv "$1" "$2" && ls -l "$2"
  • (B) rename "$1" "$2" && stat "$1"
  • (C) cp "$1" "$2" && rm "$1" && ls -l "$1"
  • (D) mv -p "$1" "$2"
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) mv "$1" "$2" && ls -l "$2"

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'mv "$1" "$2"' renames the file and 'ls -l "$2"' displays its permissions upon successful move. - (B) Running 'stat "$1"' after renaming fails with 'No such file or directory' because the old path was renamed. - (C) 'ls -l "$1"' fails because '$1' was deleted. - (D) '-p' is not a valid flag for mv.

docs.title:
Question 10: Lab 1.10: Write a shell script that creates a backup copy of '/etc/passwd' inside '/dbda/backup' named 'passwd_backup_'.
  • (A) mkdir -p /dbda/backup && cp /etc/passwd "/dbda/backup/passwd_backup_$(date +%F)"
  • (B) cp /etc/passwd /dbda/backup/passwd_backup_date
  • (C) backup /etc/passwd /dbda/backup/
  • (D) tar -cvf /dbda/backup/passwd.tar /etc/passwd
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) 

mkdir -p /dbda/backup && cp /etc/passwd "/dbda/backup/passwd_backup_$(date +%F)"

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. 'mkdir -p' ensures destination directory exists, and '$(date +%F)' evaluates to the current date (YYYY-MM-DD). - (B) Hardcodes literal string '_date' rather than evaluating the current dynamic system date. - (C) 'backup' is not a standard Linux command. - (D) Creates a tar archive without the requested specific filename format.
📑 Part 2: Conditional Logic, File Testing & System Monitoring

Question 11: Lab 2.1: Write a shell script that accepts a username as input and checks whether that user account exists on the system.
  • (A) if id "$1" &>/dev/null; then echo "User exists"; else echo "User does not exist"; fi
  • (B) if grep -q "^$1:" /etc/passwd; then echo "User exists"; else echo "User does not exist"; fi
  • (C) if [ -u "$1" ]; then echo "User exists"; fi
  • (D) Both A and B are correct implementations.
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (D) Both A and B are correct implementations.

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Valid. 'id' returns exit code 0 if user exists, non-zero if user does not exist. - (B) Valid. 'grep -q' quietly searches /etc/passwd and returns exit code 0 on match. - (C) '-u' is a file test operator for SUID permissions, not a user existence check. - (D) Correct. Both A and B are standard, robust solutions.

Question 12: Lab 2.2: Write a shell script that accepts a filename and checks whether the file exists and is readable; if so, displays its contents, otherwise displays an error message.
  • (A) if [ -f "$1" ] && [ -r "$1" ]; then cat "$1"; else echo "Error: File not found or unreadable" >&2; fi
  • (B) if [ -e "$1" ]; then cat "$1"; else echo "Error"; fi
  • (C) if [ -w "$1" ]; then cat "$1"; fi
  • (D) cat "$1" || echo "Error"
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) 

if [ -f "$1" ] && [ -r "$1" ]; then cat "$1"; else echo "Error: File not found or unreadable" >&2; fi

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. '[ -f "$1" ]' verifies regular file existence and '[ -r "$1" ]' validates read permissions before invoking cat. - (B) '-e' does not check read permissions; attempting cat on an unreadable file will trigger an unhandled permission error. - (C) '-w' checks write permission, not read permission. - (D) Does not use conditional statement syntax ('if...then...else...fi') as requested.

Question 13: Lab 2.3: Write a shell script that accepts two integer arguments ($1, $2) and prints whichever is greater, or reports that they are equal.
  • (A) if [ "$1" -gt "$2" ]; then echo "$1 is greater"; elif [ "$2" -gt "$1" ]; then echo "$2 is greater"; else echo "Numbers are equal"; fi
  • (B) if [ "$1" > "$2" ]; then echo "$1 is greater"; fi
  • (C) if [[ "$1" -ge "$2" ]]; then echo "$1 is greater"; fi
  • (D) expr "$1" > "$2"
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) 

if [ "$1" -gt "$2" ]; then echo "$1 is greater"; elif [ "$2" -gt "$1" ]; then echo "$2 is greater"; else echo "Numbers are equal"; fi

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. Uses integer comparison operators '-gt' with complete if-elif-else branches covering greater, lesser, and equality. - (B) Single bracket '[' with '>' performs ASCII string comparison and requires redirection escaping. - (C) '-ge' does not differentiate between strictly greater and equal. - (D) 'expr' evaluates mathematical expressions but does not provide the conditional report branching.

Question 14: Lab 2.4: Write a shell script that checks whether a given directory ($1) exists; if not, creates it and confirms creation, otherwise informs the user it already exists.
  • (A) if [ ! -d "$1" ]; then mkdir -p "$1" && echo "Directory created"; else echo "Directory already exists"; fi
  • (B) if [ -f "$1" ]; then echo "Exists"; else mkdir "$1"; fi
  • (C) mkdir "$1" 2>/dev/null || echo "Directory exists"
  • (D) if [ -z "$1" ]; then mkdir "$1"; fi
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) 

if [ ! -d "$1" ]; then mkdir -p "$1" && echo "Directory created"; else echo "Directory already exists"; fi

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. '[ ! -d "$1" ]' tests if directory does not exist, creating it with 'mkdir -p' and confirming success. - (B) '-f' tests for regular files, not directories. - (C) Short-circuit syntax does not differentiate between pre-existence and permission errors. - (D) '-z' tests for empty string arguments, not directory existence.

Question 15: Lab 2.5: Write a shell script that accepts a filename and checks whether the owner has read, write, and execute permissions, reporting each separately.
  • (A) [ -r "$1" ] && echo "Read: Yes" || echo "Read: No"; [ -w "$1" ] && echo "Write: Yes" || echo "Write: No"; [ -x "$1" ] && echo "Exec: Yes" || echo "Exec: No"
  • (B) ls -l "$1" | cut -c 2-4
  • (C) chmod -check "$1"
  • (D) stat -p "$1"
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A) 

[ -r "$1" ] && echo "Read: Yes" || echo "Read: No"; [ -w "$1" ] && echo "Write: Yes" || echo "Write: No"; [ -x "$1" ] && echo "Exec: Yes" || echo "Exec: No"

Option-by-Option Breakdown: - (A) Correct. Evaluates file test operators '-r', '-w', and '-x' independently and prints discrete status for each permission. - (B) Prints the raw 3-character string without discrete formatted per-permission status messages. - (C) '-check' is not a valid flag for chmod. - (D) '-p' is invalid flag syntax for stat.

Question 16: Lab 2.6: Write a shell script that checks current disk usage of the root partition ('/') and prints a warning if it has crossed 80%, otherwise prints normal status.
  • (A) USAGE=$(df / | awk 'NR==2 {gsub("%", ""); print $5}'); if [ "$USAGE" -gt 80 ]; then echo "WARNING: Disk usage high: ${USAGE}%"; else echo "Disk usage normal: ${USAGE}%"; fi
  • (B) if df / > 80%; then echo "Warning"; fi
  • (C) if [ $(du -sh /) -gt 80 ]; then echo "Warning"; fi
  • (D) df -h | grep '80%' && echo 'Warning'
Answer & Script Implementation (Click to Expand)

Correct Solution: (A)
